AKBL.summary: Askari Bank scores 80.6/100, driven mainly by fast growth (sales up 26.8% a year and EPS up 17.5% a year over three years), a 7.3% dividend yield paid in each of the last three fiscal years on record, and a share price above its 200-day average. BOP.summary: Bank of Punjab scores 79.5/100, mainly because it looks cheap (P/E 5.5 against a sector median of 6.7), pays a high dividend (10.2% yield, paid in each of the last 3 years on record) and has grown sales and earnings strongly. strengths: Cheap on earnings: P/E of 7.7 is about 0.66x the sector median of 11.6
Dividend yield of 11.2%, with a cash dividend paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record
Net margin of 13.15% is still healthy, though down from 15.56% at the start of the period
risks: Sales fell about 9% a year and EPS about 14% a year over 3 years, so the low P/E may reflect shrinking earnings
Price is below its 200-day average and trails the KSE-100 by about 25 points over a year
Debt, liquidity, cash flow and cash conversion could not be scored (no balance sheet or cash flow data), so the ability to keep paying dividends is unverified

ATRL.summary: Attock Refinery scores 56.3/100 (HOLD), held up by a very low P/E of 2.6 (about in line with the sector median of 2.4) and a share price well ahead of the KSE-100. Growth is the drag: sales have fallen about 2.6% a year and EPS about 8.9% a year over three years. Only 62% of the scorecard could be calculated, because cash flow, debt and liquidity data were missing.
strengths: Very low P/E of 2.6, close to the sector median of 2.4, so the market is paying little for each rupee of profit
FY2026 profit rebounded to Rs 22.1bn (EPS Rs 207.32) from Rs 12.0bn the year before, and net margin recovered to 6.47% from 3.97%
Share price is above its 200-day average and has beaten the KSE-100 by about 29 points over the past year
risks: Earnings are volatile and still below FY2023: EPS was Rs 274.12 then, against Rs 207.32 now, and sales are lower than in FY2024

The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash flow or working capital, which together carry 38% of the weight. A refinery can be heavily exposed to borrowing and to money owed by customers, and none of that is reflected here

A P/E this low can reflect a one-off profit, a bonus issue or a split, or a market doubt about whether earnings will last. The 1.5% yield looks small next to the latest Rs 150 per share payout (150% of face value), so the dividend figure may be stale or misleading
checks: Read the FY2026 annual report and the September 2026 quarterly results to see whether the profit rebound came from refining margins, inventory gains or one-off items
Check the balance sheet and cash flow statement for borrowings, receivables (including any amounts owed by government-linked buyers) and whether operating cash flow covers the dividends
Confirm the dividend history and the yield against the current price, and ask whether a payout of this size can be repeated

PSX.summary: The score of 56.3 (HOLD) is a split between very strong business growth and an expensive, weak-trending share price. Sales grew about 29% a year over three years, EPS rose from Rs 0.27 to Rs 2.80, and net margin climbed from 16% to 76%. Against that, the P/E of 16.2 is more than double the sector median of 7.2, and the price sits below its 200-day average and has lagged the KSE-100 by about 15 points over a year. Price-to-book, a heavily weighted factor, could not be scored, so the picture is incomplete.
strengths: Very rapid growth: sales up from Rs 1.36bn to Rs 2.94bn and profit after tax from Rs 0.22bn to Rs 2.24bn over three years (figures in Rs thousands in the data).
Net margin of 76% shows very high profitability, up from 16% at the start of the period.
Paid a cash dividend in both fiscal years on record, with a 2.1% yield.
risks: Valuation looks stretched: P/E of 16.2 versus a sector median of 7.2, and the valuation factor scored only 12.4 out of 100.
Weak price momentum: below the 200-day average and trailing the KSE-100 by 15.2 points over about a year.

The scorecard cannot see price-to-book, debt, cash flow or the sources of income. A margin this high and fast-rising may reflect market activity or one-off items that may not persist. The dividend also fell from 17% to 10% of face value, and only two years of payouts are on record.
checks: Read the FY2026 annual report for what drove the jump in revenue and margin, and how much is recurring versus one-off or tied to market conditions.
Get equity from the annual report to work out price-to-book, which the scorecard left blank, and review the balance sheet for debt and cash.
Check the September 2026 quarterly results and corporate briefing presentation to see whether growth and margins are holding, and why the dividend was lowered.

NCPL.summary: NCPL scores 56/100 (HOLD), held up mainly by a cheap valuation (P/E 7.7 vs a sector median of 11.6) and a 4.5% dividend yield. Weak sales and earnings trends pull the score down, and four factors (cash flow, debt, liquidity, cash cycle) could not be scored, so only 62% of the picture is visible.
strengths: Valuation looks low: P/E of 7.7 is about two-thirds of the sector median of 11.6
Latest year was profitable again, with a net margin of 26.3% and EPS of Rs 6.75
Pays cash dividends regularly, with a 4.5% yield and payouts in each year on record
risks: Sales fell about 19.7% a year over three years, and FY2025 showed a large loss (EPS -Rs 9.19), so earnings are very uneven

Debt, liquidity and cash flow are not scored because balance sheet and cash flow data are missing; a power producer can carry heavy borrowing and slow-paying customers, and none of that is visible here
Price is below its 200-day average, and the cheap P/E rests on one rebound year after a loss, so it may not reflect lasting earnings
checks: Look at the balance sheet for total borrowings, interest costs and how much money is owed to the company by its customers

NPL.summary: Nishat Power scores 55.4/100 (HOLD), held up mainly by a cheap valuation (P/E 7.9 vs sector median 11.6) and a steady dividend record, while shrinking sales and uneven earnings pull it down. Only 62% of the scorecard could be calculated, because debt, liquidity and cash flow data were missing, so the score is incomplete.
strengths: Valuation looks low: P/E of 7.9 is about 0.68x the sector median of 11.6.
Cash dividends were paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years, with a 4.1% yield.
Net margin in FY2026 was 22.53%, higher than 17.73% in FY2023, and the share price has beaten the KSE-100 by about 41 points over roughly a year.
risks: Sales fell about 21.8% a year over 3 years (from Rs 23.1bn to Rs 11.0bn), and FY2025 had a loss of Rs 747m.
Earnings are volatile: EPS swung from 15.22 to -2.11 to 7.01, so the current low P/E rests on a single recovery year and may not be a reliable guide.

The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash conversion or cash flow, which together carry 38% of the weight. For a power producer these matter, including whether profits are actually collected in cash. The price is also below its 200-day average.
checks: Check the annual report's cash flow statement and receivables to see whether profits are being turned into cash, and whether payments from customers are delayed.
Look at borrowings, repayment schedules and cash on the balance sheet to judge whether the dividend is affordable.
Find out why sales fell and why FY2025 made a loss (e.g. plant contract terms, capacity payments, one-off items), and whether FY2026 is a sustainable level.

LUCK.summary: Lucky Cement scores 51.4 out of 100 (HOLD). Strong sales growth and a much higher net margin (14.3% to 34.2% over the period) are offset by a P/E of 13.2, about 1.5 times the sector median of 8.7. The score also rests on only 62% of the data: debt, cash flow and liquidity could not be assessed, so it is less reliable than the number suggests.
strengths: Sales grew about 12.5% a year over three years, from Rs 95.8bn to Rs 136.5bn.
Profit after tax rose from Rs 13.7bn to Rs 46.6bn, and net margin improved every year.
Cash dividends were paid in both years on record, with the latest at 250% of face value, up from 200%.
risks: The shares trade at a premium to the cement sector (P/E 13.2 vs 8.7), which leaves less room for disappointment if the high margins fall back.
Debt, cash flow quality, liquidity and cash conversion are unscored (38% of the weight), so leverage and whether profits turn into cash are unknown.
The share price lagged the KSE-100 by about 7.9 points over the past year, and the dividend yield is only 1.2%.
checks: Reconcile EPS with profit after tax across years. Look for changes in share count, bonus shares, restatements, or consolidated versus standalone figures.
Read the balance sheet and cash flow statement for borrowings, interest cover and operating cash flow against the Rs 46.6bn profit.
Find out what drove the jump in net margin to 34%, such as one-off gains, other income, or associate and investment earnings, and whether it can last.
